catalog_quote: The following rules are concerned with the placement of accent in words. Such rules must account for the fact that a word will only have one accent mark in the terminal string (unless there is no inherent accent in any of the constituent forms). The placement of that accent is a function of the inherent accents and their relationship to each other and junctures. [pp. 47-48] ... Rule 24 ... Occasional single syllable forms may appear. Innate accent for all forms is on the penult. Hence a form with only one syllable is given by the dictionary in the form ´S. If such a form is given by the syntax directly following a # or // juncture, accent is progressive to the only syllable of the form. new_statements.quote: Occasional single syllable forms may appear. Innate accent for all forms is on the penult. Hence a form with only one syllable is given by the dictionary in the form ´S. If such a form is given by the syntax directly following a # or // juncture, accent is progressive to the only syllable of the form. [p. 48] ... This is the rule for zeroing all remaining innate accents within a word but the last one. [p. 50] ... There are two inherent kinds of accent. ` is weaker, disappearing in a word when preceded by a strong accent. ´ is strong inherent accent which is only zeroed in a word where it is followed by a strong accent, unless // juncture should come between them. Accent is phonetically an intensification of the signal in relation to surrounding syllables, plus a higher pitch, plus slight lengthening of the vowel and surrounding consonants. [p. 28]

new_statements.rule_in_words: Every lexical formative (verb stem, noun stem, adverb, verbal suffix, particle) carries an inherent accent on its penultimate syllable; a monosyllabic stem projects its accent onto the syllable immediately preceding it (e.g. a prefix: #o-ken# > #ó-ken#) or, word-initially, onto itself. Within the phonological word all inherent accents except the last one are deleted, so each word surfaces with a single primary accent: on the penult of the last accented formative, which in the cited examples is the penultimate syllable of the word (#o-apo-póta#, #o-apo-pam-tar-áme#, #ó-ken#, #ʔáŋ-a#). Harrison 1975 (p. 41, p. 120) gives the same rule in Portuguese: 'O acento cai na penúltima sílaba de todo tema nominal', 'Coloca-se este acento gráfico na penúltima sílaba, seja real ou imaginário'.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Harrison 1975 rule 18 (p. 120): postpositions/relators (relacionadores) carry a secondary accent (`) on their penult; it is deleted when a primary accent is present in the relational phrase and promoted to primary when it is the only accent (Harrison 1971 Rules 27-28, pp. 49-50: #ʔáŋ-a-pìpe# > #ʔáŋ-a-pipe#; #i-pìpe# > #i-pípe#). Phrase-level pitch/intonation are explicitly left undescribed (1975 §2.11, p. 15).
new_statements.exceptions: Some formatives have no inherent accent (D, past-tense words, other subjunctives, the nominal marker A per 1975 rule 18). In possessor//possessed noun sequences (// juncture) both nouns keep their accent (1971 Rule 24 note, p. 48). Weak-accented postpositions lose their accent after an accented syllable, so a word like ʔáŋ-a-pipe surfaces with accent on its first syllable rather than the word penult. Accent regresses to the final syllable of the preceding form across = and - junctures (Rules 25-26).
new_statements.domain_note: Describes slow-speech citation pronunciation of words (the paper's stated scope). The rule is stem-level penultimate accent computed morphologically, then reduced to one accent per phonological word (#..#), so the surface word accent is the penult of the last accent-bearing formative, not always the penult of the whole word. Sentence/phrase stress and intonation are not described.
new_statements.identity_note: Both Harrison works describe the Asurini of the Trocará post on the Tocantins (Tucuruí, Pará), i.e. toca1235 [asu], based on fieldwork 1962-69. Not the Xingu Asurini (asn, xing1240): Nicholson 1978 'Aspectos da língua assuriní', named in the earlier scan note, is tagged asn in hh.bib and should not be counted for this language.

sources.locator: p. 48 (Rule 24) and p. 50 (Rule 29); accent defined p. 28. PDF pages 58, 60, 38 of the archive.org scan.
sources.note: p. 28: two inherent accents (weak ` and strong ´); accent = intensity + higher pitch + slight lengthening. p. 48 Rule 24: 'Innate accent for all forms is on the penult'; monosyllabic forms get accent on the preceding syllable (or on themselves after # or //). Rules 25-29 (pp. 49-50): accent regresses across = and - junctures, weak-accented postpositions lose accent after another accented syllable, and all innate accents in a word but the last are zeroed; both nouns keep accent in possessor//possessed constructions. Verified against page images (pp. 28, 48, 50).
